segments.say: Now picture the river, dark and slow and wide, flowing quietly through the middle of the town. The path along its bank is lined with old iron lamps, and their light lies on the water in long golden ribbons that wobble and stretch and gently shiver as the river slides by underneath them.

Listen for the sound of the river. It's very soft, a low, steady murmur, almost like breathing. The water moves past the stones of the bank with a quiet lapping sound, over and over, never stopping, never hurrying. It's been making this sound every night for hundreds of years, and it will go on making it long after tonight.

Let your breathing find the rhythm of the water. As the river flows, breathe in, slowly, all the way down. And as it flows on, breathe out, slowly, all the way. You don't need to make it perfect. Just let the river set the pace, slow and easy, and let your breath follow along behind it.

Picture the two ducks on the low stone wall, just where Elena saw them. They're still asleep, heads tucked under their wings, feathers fluffed up against the cold. Every so often, one of them shifts a little and settles again, without waking.

show.cap: Two ducks asleep by the river

segments.say: Underneath all those soft feathers, the ducks are perfectly warm. The cold air can't reach them. They've made a little world of warmth for themselves, and they rest in it, quite safe, quite content. You've made a little world of warmth for yourself too, in your bed, under your covers. You can rest in it, just as they do.

Picture a few small rowing boats tied up along the bank, moored for the night. They rock very gently on the slow water, nudging against the stones, then drifting back, then nudging again. Each one has a little pool of frost in the bottom. Their oars are tucked neatly inside. They rock, and rock, and rest.

You might picture yourself lying in one of those boats, wrapped up in a thick, warm blanket, rocking ever so gently on the water. The rope holds you safely to the bank. The river moves softly underneath. The stars are above you. There's nothing to do but feel the slow, gentle rocking, side to side, side to side.

Further along the bank, a grey heron stands at the water's edge, perfectly still, on one long leg. It might be asleep. It might be just resting. It doesn't move a single feather. It just stands there, tall and quiet in the moonlight, as patient as the river itself. You can be as still as the heron.

Picture walking slowly along the river path, from lamp to lamp. Each one is old and black, with a glass lantern on top, and a soft golden glow inside. You reach one, and pass it, and walk on into the gentle dark, and then the next one appears ahead, waiting. There's always another lamp ahead, all the way along the river.

Picture a single leaf floating on the dark water, a brown leaf left over from autumn. It drifts along slowly with the current, turning a little, this way, then that way. It doesn't steer. It doesn't need to. The river carries it, gently, wherever it's going. You can let yourself be carried like that too.

Imagine you're as light as that leaf, resting on the surface of the slow, calm water. The river holds you up. You don't need to do anything at all. You don't need to swim or steer or think. Just float, and drift, and let the gentle current carry you along, under the lamps, through the quiet night.

On the far side of the river, there's a row of tall, dark trees, their bare branches reaching up into the starry sky. They stand very still. There's no wind tonight. Just the trees, and the stars behind them, and the slow river in front, all quiet together, keeping each other company through the long night.

And now, picture the moon rising slowly over the trees, round and pale and silver. Its light joins the lamplight on the water, so there are ribbons of gold and a wide path of silver, all shimmering together on the river. It's very beautiful, and very calm. You can look at it for as long as you like.

As you watch the moonlight on the water, you might notice that your body feels heavier now, sinking a little further into the bed. Your thoughts might feel softer, further away, like voices in another room. That's all right. That's what happens as you drift towards sleep. Let it happen, gently.

Up ahead, the old green footbridge crosses the river, its iron rail glittering faintly with frost under the lamps. Picture walking slowly towards it, along the quiet path, with the river murmuring beside you and the moon above. There's no hurry. You'll get there when you get there.
